title: The Brahmanas' Wives Bring Food to Krishna
story:
The boys came back empty-handed, and when they told Krishna what had happened — that the brahmanas had neither refused nor agreed, that they had simply gone on with their rites as though no one had spoken — the master of the whole world only laughed. There was no anger in it. He did not scold the men, and he did not repeat the request. He simply said: go to their wives, and tell them that I have come, with Balarama.

So the boys went a second time, now to the women's quarters of those same houses. There the wives sat, well-adorned in their own homes, going about the quiet work of the afternoon. The boys bowed to them and spoke with the same respect as before: Obeisance to you, wives of the brahmanas; listen to our words. While pasturing the cows with the cowherds, he has come from far away, with Balarama — and he is hungry.

The wives heard the name, and everything in them rose at once. They had always longed for the sight of Krishna; the verses say the longing was constant, something they carried every day without speaking it aloud. They had heard of him — the dark boy of Vrindavan whose name was on everyone's lips — and they had kept that longing lit like a lamp in a dark room. Now, without a word of hesitation, they began to fill vessels with food — food of four kinds, rich and fine, prepared with care — and they hurried out toward him. In that sudden movement there was something of a festival — doors flung open, feet hurrying, voices rising — as though the whole women's quarter had been waiting all along for exactly this summons.

Their husbands tried to stop them. Their brothers tried, their kinsmen tried, their own sons called after them from the doorways, asking where they thought they were going and before whom. They called it madness, or worse; they reminded the women of their duties, their good names, the scandal of it. But the women did not slow. A longing kept secret for years has a force that reproach cannot match, and the verses are clear that not one of them turned back. The text reaches for water to say what they were like: they went as rivers run to the sea, drawn by a pull that nothing in the house could answer.

It is worth pausing on what they left behind. Not small things — houses, husbands, the regard of kin, the settled shape of a whole life. And they left it all without a backward look, because the one thing they had wanted without daring to ask for it had finally come within reach. And yet the text gives the moment no weight of tragedy; there is only eagerness in it. The women are not fleeing a prison; they are running toward a light they have waited for, and the running itself is a kind of arrival. They did not need to be told the way; they had walked it a thousand times in their thoughts.

So through the groves of Vrindavan they went, their vessels bright in their hands, their veils and bracelets catching the afternoon light, their faces all turned one way — toward the place where Krishna waited with Balarama and the boys and the grazing cows. Some carried the food balanced high; others held it close against them, as though afraid the afternoon might end before they arrived.

It had taken the men an afternoon of silence to answer him. It took their wives no more than a breath.
reflection: The contrast is the point of the story. The learned brahmanas saw only a herd-boy and sent him away; their wives, who had no learning to lean on and only longing to go by, saw what the longing had prepared them to see. They drop everything — home, kin, reputation — because the one they have wanted is finally near.
next_story_tease: But when the wives reached him, they would refuse to go back at all.
hero_scene: The brahmana wives hurrying through the groves of Vrindavan with bright vessels of food in their hands, their husbands and kinsmen calling them back in vain, their faces turned toward the place where Krishna and Balarama wait with the grazing cows.
